solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Spiteful as the American elite?

definitions.note: a cryptic reading: like a WASP, so WASP-ish

blocks.note: first meaning: irritable and malicious
second meaning, split as a suffix word: in the manner of a White Anglo-Saxon Protestant

explanation.walkthrough: A WASP is a White Anglo-Saxon Protestant, shorthand for the old American upper class; the question mark flags the made-up sense of WASP plus -ish.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone stinging and irritable is compared to a wasp, so the adjective describes a sharp, peevish temper.

clue.text: Big guns buggered up literary festival's finale

indicators.note: something buggered up is wrecked and disordered, so the letters lose their order
a finale is the closing part, so only the last letter of the word is used

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of festival

explanation.surface: A book festival ends in chaos, its closing session blown apart as if by heavy guns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big guns' could mean important people at the festival, but here it is literal heavy weaponry.
explanation.definitionFit: Artillery is the collective term for large-calibre mounted weapons such as cannon and howitzers.

clue.text: ... as a pikestaff left in arse

definitions.note: the answer completes the phrase 'plain as a pikestaff'

indicators.note: a thing placed in something else sits inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: from 'pain in the arse', a nuisance; Cyclops treats the two as interchangeable
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A rude continuation of the previous clue, as if a pikestaff had been put somewhere painful.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots tie the clue to a familiar phrase: 'plain as a pikestaff' means obvious. PAIN stands for arse via the idiom 'pain in the arse'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'plain as a pikestaff' means perfectly obvious, so the missing word is the adjective meaning clear or evident.

clue.text: see 14ac.
One raring to go off – "Charge!"

indicators.note: something that goes off explodes or spoils, so these letters are blown into a new order

blocks.note: one is the indefinite article a
taken as written

explanation.surface: An eager cavalryman, keen to set off, shouts the order to charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge!' reads as a battle cry, but the definition is the legal verb: to charge someone formally in court.
explanation.definitionFit: To arraign is to bring a person before a court to answer a formal accusation, a legal sense of charging.

clue.text: After little resistance, Bush surprisingly grabs sexually unfussy person's balls

indicators.note: a surprising result is an unexpected one, so the letters turn up in an unexpected order
to grab is to seize and hold, so one piece is clutched inside another

blocks.note: R is the symbol for electrical resistance, 'little' signalling the abbreviation
taken as written
BI is short for bisexual

explanation.surface: A smutty image of a President Bush grabbing someone's private parts after token resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places R in front. 'Balls' looks like part of the smut, but it is the definition in its slang sense of nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang 'balls' means nonsense or worthless talk, which is exactly what calling something rubbish asserts.

clue.text: PS. we conflicted with old fart with political allegiance changing

indicators.note: a conflicted mind is torn and muddled, so the letters are jumbled
switching political allegiance means moving from left to right, so one side's letter is swapped for the other's

blocks.note: taken as written
the L (left) in old becomes R (right)
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rude postscript about falling out with an old buffer who has defected to another party.
explanation.walkthrough: L and R stand for left and right, so the defection swaps one letter for the other before everything is mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: A PS (postscript) is text added after the main body of a letter, a kind of closing note or afterword.

clue.text: Stuff ex-pop star, Michael – no end of pretence

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that letter is taken
'no' says the following item is absent, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: George Michael, formerly of Wham!, here giving his first name
the final letter of pretence

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on George Michael, the late pop singer, and his pretensions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Michael' is a surname here, so the pop star's first name is wanted; one E is dropped from it.
explanation.definitionFit: To stuff yourself is to eat greedily to excess, which is the verb sense of gorging.

clue.text: Detesting worn out British government

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or not in place, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A weary public loathing a tired, exhausted government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worn out' reads as one phrase, but 'worn' is letters and 'out' alone signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Downing Street, home of the Prime Minister's residence at Number 10, is used as a metonym for the British government.

clue.text: Prescott, a waffler, hoarding capital

indicators.note: to hoard is to keep something stored away inside, so the letters lie within the words

blocks.note: runs across the end of Prescott, a, and the start of waffler

explanation.surface: John Prescott, Labour's rambling former deputy prime minister, sitting on a pile of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' tempts as money being hoarded, but it is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Ottawa is the capital city of Canada, an example of the category named by the definition.

clue.text: Alternative Tyson type of spacecraft?

blocks.note: or introduces an alternative
boxer Mike Tyson notoriously bit Evander Holyfield's ear in 1997

explanation.surface: A whimsical suggestion that another Mike Tyson might be a kind of spaceship.
explanation.walkthrough: Tyson is defined by his most infamous act, biting an opponent's ear during a title fight.
explanation.definitionFit: An orbiter is a spacecraft designed to circle a planet or moon rather than land on it.

clue.text: Sank windy island, drowning large white supremacist

indicators.note: a windy road twists and turns, so these letters are twisted out of order
to drown something is to submerge it, so one piece goes underneath, inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: A shipwreck in which a stormy island seems to have sunk and drowned someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled first word takes in L, and the island follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A Klansman is a member of the Ku Klux Klan, the American group preaching white racial supremacy.

clue.text: State: "I'd back away from the PM"

indicators.note: to back away from something is to withdraw from it, so letters are taken out of the word

blocks.note: Benjamin Disraeli, Victorian prime minister
the letters I and D

explanation.surface: A politician's quoted vow to distance themselves from the Prime Minister's stance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The PM' sounds like the current one, but it is DISRAELI; removing its outer I and D leaves ISRAEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Israel is a sovereign country in the Middle East, an example of a nation state.

clue.text: (& 4dn.) "Strike off member!" – Brenda (Corbyn follower)

indicators.note: something off is out of place or gone bad, so the letters are disarranged

blocks.note: taken as written
a limb is a member of the body
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth, whose royal cipher is ER

explanation.surface: A call to expel a party member, credited to someone called Brenda, about Labour's new leader.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye has long called the Queen 'Brenda', so it yields the royal cipher ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Keir Starmer succeeded Jeremy Corbyn as leader of the Labour Party in 2020, so he literally followed him.

clue.text: Topless lager lout pissed on last of beer ('Governor')

indicators.note: topless means with the top removed, so the first letter goes
the last of a word is its final letter, so only that letter is taken
pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunk letters stagger out of order

blocks.note: lager without its first letter
taken as written
the final letter of beer

explanation.surface: A shirtless, drunken lager lout at the end of a night's drinking, perhaps confronting a governor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed' is British slang for drunk, not angry as in American usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A governor in engineering is a device controlling speed or flow, which is a type of regulator.

clue.text: Have a stab at rehearsal

definitions.note: the verb 'run through', to pierce with a blade

blocks.note: first meaning: to pierce someone with a sword
second meaning: a practice performance from start to finish

explanation.walkthrough: 'Have a stab at' usually means attempt, which suits a rehearsal; here it is literal stabbing with a sword.
explanation.definitionFit: To run someone through is to impale them with a blade, and a full practice of a show is also called a run-through.

clue.text: Lofty rejected Regina at the point of getting married (disputed territory)

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: lofty means tall, hence big
R stands for Regina, Latin for queen
a wedding takes place at the altar

explanation.surface: A tall suitor jilted by Regina at the altar, with a hint of territorial squabbling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lofty' reads as a nickname for a tall man; as a word it gives BIG, sent backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Gibraltar is a British overseas territory whose sovereignty Spain has long contested.

clue.text: Organ good, girls? Prescription item

definitions.note: singular in the clue; the answer is a plural noun naming one item

blocks.note: the eye is an organ of the body
G is the abbreviation for good
lasses are girls

explanation.surface: A doctor asking young women whether an organ is healthy before writing a prescription.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prescription item' suggests medicine, but optical prescriptions are also written.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyeglasses are spectacles made to an optician's prescription to correct a person's vision.

clue.text: Old-fashioned, sly CIA scheme

indicators.note: to scheme is to plot and arrange, so these letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: arch means knowing or mischievously sly
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cunning but outdated plot by the American intelligence agency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scheme' reads as a noun for the plot; it works as a verb telling us to rearrange the agency's initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaic describes something belonging to an earlier era and now out of date, a synonym for old-fashioned.

clue.text: Ulcers, unfortunately, limiting a lay

indicators.note: unfortunate things go wrong, so the letters end up in the wrong order
to limit is to set bounds around something, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A painful ailment putting a stop to someone's sex life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay' reads as a sexual encounter; it is the adjective meaning not belonging to the clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay people are those outside the clergy, so a lay matter is non-religious, the sense of secular.

clue.text: see 22ac.
(& 21ac.) Abandoned BBC led up it – the nation's burden

indicators.note: abandoned can mean wild and unrestrained, so the letters run loose

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grumble that the BBC, funded by the licence fee, is a costly burden on the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandoned' looks like it describes the BBC; it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Public debt is the money a government owes, a liability carried by the whole country and its taxpayers.

clue.text: Old tax applied after raise? Piss off!

blocks.note: to up something is to raise it
Selective Employment Tax, a UK payroll tax of 1966 to 1973

explanation.surface: An angry response to a tax rise.
explanation.walkthrough: SET was the Selective Employment Tax, a short-lived British levy on employers; 'applied after' puts it second.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang to piss someone off is to annoy or anger them, which is to upset them.

clue.text: Transport member stripped of power, wash-out

indicators.note: to strip something of an item is to take that item off, so a letter is removed
out can mean out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: slang for the male member
P is the symbol for power
taken as written

explanation.surface: A transport minister sacked and left powerless, the whole thing a wash-out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transport member' suggests a Transport Secretary, but 'Transport' alone is the definition and 'member' is the crude slang word.
explanation.definitionFit: A rickshaw is a light two-wheeled passenger cart pulled by a person, a form of transport.

clue.text: Figure is rejected by Times – Tory party gutted

indicators.note: a rejected thing is sent back, so the word is read backwards
gutting removes the insides, so only the outer letters remain

blocks.note: taken as written
X is the multiplication sign
the Tory party, that is the word Tory, with its middle removed

explanation.surface: A newspaper turning down a figure while the Conservative party lies devastated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper, and 'gutted' like dismay; they are the multiplication sign and an emptied word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sixty is a number, and figure is a common word for any number.

clue.text: Was an MP one put away and stuff?

blocks.note: an MP sits in Parliament, so one who was an MP sat
I is the Roman numeral one
to put away food is to eat it

explanation.surface: A cynical question: does being an MP mean being jailed and stuffing your pockets?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put away' suggests imprisonment; it is the informal sense of eating heartily.
explanation.definitionFit: To satiate someone is to fill them to the point of fullness, the same as stuffing them with food.

clue.text: Freedom of non-professionals to grab a kiss

indicators.note: to grab is to seize and hold, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: the laity are ordinary people without specialist training
X is the kiss written at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: Amateurs enjoying the liberty to steal a kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: The laity originally meant non-clergy, and by extension anyone outside a profession.
explanation.definitionFit: Laxity means looseness or lack of strictness, a looser sense of freedom from rules.

clue.text: Draw thanks for backing sources of terrible Republican legislation

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the word is read in reverse
a source is where something starts, so first letters are taken

blocks.note: ta is British informal for thanks
the first letters of the two words
an act is a piece of legislation

explanation.surface: A politician earning gratitude for supporting dreadful Republican laws.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is everyday British slang for thank you; 'backing' sounds like political support but sends it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To attract is to pull or draw something towards you, as a magnet or a crowd-pleaser does.

clue.text: What to say when you're about to choke contestants wanting a change of side?

definitions.text: What to say when you're about to choke

indicators.note: changing side means swapping left for right, so one side's letter replaces the other's

blocks.note: players compete in a contest; its L (left) becomes R (right)

explanation.surface: Sporting advice for players about to bottle it, perhaps hoping to transfer to another team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Choke' is sporting slang for failing under pressure, but read literally it is dying, when people say their prayers.
explanation.definitionFit: People facing death traditionally say their prayers, so these are the words spoken when about to die.
